title: Optical-Fluorescence Decomposition Reveals Progressive Multimodal Divergence with Histologic Severity of Occlusal Caries.
html:
Background: Occlusal caries remains difficult to characterize because surface changes do not always reflect demineralization depth. Quantitative light-induced fluorescence (QLF) provides complementary information through fluorescence loss and red fluorescence, but these features are typically evaluated independently of white-light appearance. Joint analysis of paired images may reveal modality-specific changes associated with lesion progression. This study developed an interpretable optical-fluorescence decomposition framework to quantify multimodal divergence and assess its relationship with histologic caries severity.

Methods: Paired white-light optical and QLF images of 94 occlusal tooth surfaces were spatially registered and restricted to the corresponding region. Optical and QLF red, green, and blue (RGB) channels were jointly represented as a six-channel vector and standardized before principal component analysis, retaining four components. Optical and QLF loading magnitudes were combined into a Modality Dominance Index (MDI), with positive and negative values indicating relative QLF and optical dominance, respectively. A tooth-level Optical-Fluorescence Divergence Index (OFDI) was defined as the range between the maximum and minimum MDI values across components. OFDI and related component-level descriptors were evaluated against histologic severity using nonparametric trend, pairwise, and receiver operating characteristic analyses.

Results: The OFDI increased progressively from sound surfaces, outer-enamel involvement, inner-enamel involvement, and dentin involvement (0.248±0.110, 0.302±0.180, 0.419±0.217, and 0.650±0.210, respectively) and was significantly associated with histologic severity (Spearman's ρ=0.483, p<0.001). The largest adjacent-group difference was between enamel and dentin caries (Holm-adjusted p=0.009; Cliff's δ=0.575). The OFDI showed increasing discrimination with depth, with AUCs of 0.705 for any histologic caries, 0.739 for inner-enamel involvement or deeper, and 0.855 for dentin caries. For dentin caries, sensitivity was 83.3%, and specificity was 75.6%.

Conclusions: The joint optical-fluorescence decomposition framework quantitatively captured modality divergence associated with increasing histologic caries severity. The OFDI increased progressively with lesion depth and showed its strongest discrimination for advanced histologic involvement, supporting its potential as an imaging biomarker of optical-fluorescence heterogeneity. These findings suggest that paired analysis of conventional optical and QLF images may provide complementary information on lesion severity beyond single-modality assessment.
